heading: Environment variables for handlers
body:
`ty` clears the environment of every handler process, so a handler cannot read the variables of the shell that started `ty`. It gets only a small baseline: `PATH`, `LANG`, `LC_ALL` and `TMPDIR` on Unix, and `PATH`, `PATHEXT`, `SYSTEMROOT`, `WINDIR`, `COMSPEC`, `TEMP` and `TMP` on Windows. Configuration, not code, decides what else a handler sees.

Cloud SDKs and many tools read their credentials and settings from the environment. List those variables in `server.environment` in `server/application.json`. An entry is a name, such as `HOME`, or a prefix pattern that ends in `*`, such as `AWS_*` or `HD_*`. With the list below, `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` and `HD_REGION` reach handlers in every Yon language as ordinary environment variables: `process.env` in JavaScript, `os.environ` in Python, `os.Getenv` in Go, `System.getenv` in Java, and so on. A variable that the list does not name, such as `OTHER_SECRET`, does not reach them. Gateway commands, relay programs and Yon test units under `ty test` get the same list. The list is empty unless you set it. This is Spring's externalized configuration, bound explicitly: the application says which variables it uses, and it reads nothing else.

`*` alone would pass every variable, so the server refuses to start with `TY2010`. It also refuses any entry that names or covers a variable that `ty` itself owns: `TAC_*`, `TACHYON_*`, `YON_*`, and the proxy variables that the outgoing request guard sets (`HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `ALL_PROXY`, `NO_PROXY` and `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY`). So `T*` and `NO_*` are refused too. Names are compared without regard to case.

The configuration holds names, never values. The values stay in the environment of `ty`; `ty` never writes them to the configuration, to its logs or to a diagnostic, and a refused entry is reported by its name only. Every handler of the application can read an allowed variable, so list only what the handlers need. Settings that belong to the application, such as a database password, still go in `.env` as `YON_` names (see Settings and configuration). ADR 0026 explains the choice. The example controller is written in Go. A handler in JavaScript, TypeScript, Python, PHP, Java, Groovy, C#, F#, Kotlin, Rust, Dart, Ruby, Lua or C++ reads an allowed variable with its own environment API in the same way, so this section shows Go only.
